```{r setup, include = FALSE}

find_proj_root <- function(path = getwd()) {
  path <- normalizePath(path)
  repeat {
    if (length(list.files(path, pattern = "\\.Rproj$"))) return(path)
    parent <- dirname(path)
    if (parent == path) stop("No .Rproj file found above ", getwd())
    path <- parent
  }
```

```{r load}
source(file.path(proj_root, "R", "utils_data.R"))
source(file.path(proj_root, "R", "utils_models.R"))
source(file.path(proj_root, "R", "utils_classify.R"))
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(knitr)
  library(MASS, exclude = "select")   # lda, qda (exclude 'select' so dplyr's select still works)
  library(class)                      # knn
  library(rpart)
  library(rpart.plot)
  library(glmnet)
  library(ranger)
})
N_CORES <- max(1, parallel::detectCores() - 1)
for (d in c(paths$fig_rq3, paths$tab_rq3, paths$models_rq3)) dir.create(d, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

rq3   <- readRDS(file.path(paths$processed, "rq3_model_data.rds"))
dat   <- rq3$data
feats <- rq3$features
Y     <- "rise"
train <- dat |> filter(split == "train")     # feature years 1996-2016
test  <- dat |> filter(split == "test")      # feature years 2017-2024: used once, in section 6

# time-ordered folds: train on all years before a two-year block, validate on the block
folds <- make_time_folds(train$year, valid_blocks = list(2009:2010, 2011:2012, 2013:2014, 2015:2016))
sapply(folds, \(f) c(train_rows = length(f$train), valid_rows = length(f$valid)))
```

# Purpose and plan

Step 1 built 1,914 district-years (66 districts, feature years 1996–2024) with eleven features known at the end of
each year, and the label "did new dwellings rise the following year?". Here we fit classifiers, from the simplest to
the most flexible, and compare them:

| Model | What it does | Tuned settings |
|---|---|---|
| Baselines | majority class; "same direction as this year"; "opposite of this year" | none |
| Logistic regression | models the log-odds of a rise as a straight-line combination of the features | none |
| Lasso logistic regression | the same, with a penalty that shrinks weak coefficients to zero | penalty λ |
| LDA | assumes each class is a normal cloud with the same shape; draws a straight boundary | none |
| QDA | as LDA, but each class has its own shape; curved boundary | none |
| Classification tree | splits on thresholds into groups that are mostly rise or mostly fall | `cp`, `minbucket` |
| k-nearest neighbours | votes of the *k* most similar training district-years | *k* |
| Random forest | many trees on bootstrap samples, averaged | `mtry`, `min.node.size` |

The pitch named logistic regression, LDA and a tree. QDA and lasso are natural extensions of logistic regression
and LDA; KNN and the random forest test whether a flexible model finds structure the linear ones miss.

**Ground rules (as in RQ1).** Tuning and model choice use time-ordered cross-validation on the training years only.
The test years (2017–2024) are used once. Every model outputs a **probability** of a rise; a district-year is
classified as "rise" when that probability is above 0.5.

# How models are scored

| Metric | Meaning | Good |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | share of district-years classified correctly | high |
| Sensitivity | share of actual rises predicted as rises | high |
| Specificity | share of actual falls predicted as falls | high |
| Balanced accuracy | mean of sensitivity and specificity; not fooled by predicting one class | high |
| **AUC** | probability that a random rise gets a higher predicted probability than a random fall; does not depend on the 0.5 threshold | 0.5 = guessing, 1 = perfect |
| Brier score | mean squared difference between the probability and the 0/1 outcome | low (0.25 = always saying 50%) |

Models are tuned and compared on **CV AUC**, because it measures how well the probabilities rank rises above falls
without depending on a threshold.

# Fitting and tuning the models

Each model is written as a function that fits on one data set and returns probabilities for another, so all
models go through the same folds and metrics (`cv_tune_class()` in `R/utils_classify.R`).

```{r factories}
fml <- reformulate(feats, response = Y)
x_of <- function(df) as.matrix(df[feats])

fp_majority  <- function(tr, nw, p) rep(mean(tr[[Y]]), nrow(nw))
fp_same      <- function(tr, nw, p) as.numeric(nw$growth_1y > 0)     # rose this year -> rise next year
fp_opposite  <- function(tr, nw, p) as.numeric(nw$growth_1y <= 0)    # fell this year -> rise next year

fp_logistic  <- function(tr, nw, p) predict(glm(fml, data = tr, family = binomial), newdata = nw, type = "response")

lambda_grid <- 10^seq(-1, -5, length.out = 60)
fp_lasso <- function(tr, nw, p) {
  fit  <- glmnet(x_of(tr), tr[[Y]], family = "binomial", alpha = 1, lambda = lambda_grid)
  pred <- predict(fit, x_of(nw), type = "response")
  colnames(pred) <- fit$lambda
  pred
}

fp_lda <- function(tr, nw, p) predict(lda(fml, data = tr), newdata = nw)$posterior[, "1"]
fp_qda <- function(tr, nw, p) predict(qda(fml, data = tr), newdata = nw)$posterior[, "1"]

fp_tree <- function(tr, nw, p) {
  fit <- rpart(update(fml, factor(rise) ~ .), data = tr, method = "class",
               control = rpart.control(cp = p$cp, minbucket = p$minbucket, xval = 0))
  predict(fit, newdata = nw, type = "prob")[, "1"]
}

fp_knn <- function(tr, nw, p) {
  centre <- colMeans(x_of(tr)); spread <- apply(x_of(tr), 2, sd)     # scale with the TRAINING means and SDs
  xs_tr <- scale(x_of(tr), centre, spread); xs_nw <- scale(x_of(nw), centre, spread)
  set.seed(462)                                                       # knn breaks ties at random
  # use.all = FALSE: exactly k neighbours even when several are at the same distance
  pred <- knn(xs_tr, xs_nw, cl = factor(tr[[Y]]), k = p$k, prob = TRUE, use.all = FALSE)
  share_winner <- attr(pred, "prob")
  if_else(pred == "1", share_winner, 1 - share_winner)                # probability of a rise
}

fp_rf <- function(tr, nw, p) {
  fit <- ranger(update(fml, factor(rise) ~ .), data = tr, probability = TRUE, num.trees = 500,
                mtry = p$mtry, min.node.size = p$min.node.size, num.threads = N_CORES, seed = 462)
  predict(fit, data = nw)$predictions[, "1"]
}
```

```{r tune, cache = TRUE}
tune <- function(fp, grid = NULL, inner = NULL) timed(cv_tune_class(fp, grid, train, folds, Y, inner))
res <- list(
  "Majority class"          = tune(fp_majority),
  "Same as this year"       = tune(fp_same),
  "Opposite of this year"   = tune(fp_opposite),
  "Logistic regression"     = tune(fp_logistic),
  "Lasso logistic"          = tune(fp_lasso, inner = "lambda"),
  "LDA"                     = tune(fp_lda),
  "QDA"                     = tune(fp_qda),
  "Classification tree"     = tune(fp_tree, expand_grid(cp = c(0.0005, 0.001, 0.002, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05),
                                                        minbucket = c(10, 30, 60))),
  "k-nearest neighbours"    = tune(fp_knn, tibble(k = c(5, 11, 21, 41, 81, 121, 201, 301, 451))),
  "Random forest"           = tune(fp_rf, expand_grid(mtry = c(2, 3, 5, 8), min.node.size = c(5, 20, 50)))
)
```

```{r cv-table}
model_order <- names(res)
cv_all <- imap_dfr(res, summarise_class_tuning) |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = model_order))
# later cached chunks depend on the tuning results: re-run them whenever these change
knitr::opts_chunk$set(cache.extra = list(file_md5, rlang::hash(cv_all)))
save_tab(cv_all, "t03_cv_results", dir = paths$tab_rq3) |>
  select(model, best_settings, cv_auc, cv_auc_se, cv_accuracy, cv_balanced_accuracy, cv_brier) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Cross-validation (validation years 2009–2016), best setting of each model")
```

```{r tuning-curves, fig.height = 3.4}
p_tune <- bind_rows(
  res[["k-nearest neighbours"]]$summary |> transmute(model = "k-nearest neighbours: k", x = k, cv_auc),
  res[["Lasso logistic"]]$summary |> transmute(model = "Lasso: log10(λ)", x = log10(lambda), cv_auc)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, cv_auc)) + geom_line(colour = "#2a6f97") + geom_point(colour = "#2a6f97", size = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~model, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "Effect of the main tuning setting on cross-validated AUC", x = NULL, y = "CV AUC")
save_fig(p_tune, "fig03_tuning_curves", dir = paths$fig_rq3, height = 3.4, width = 8)
```

**Observation.** * **The baselines are weak.** "Same direction as this year" is *worse* than guessing (CV AUC 0.45), and "opposite
  of this year" is only slightly better (0.55). A district that rose this year is a little more likely to fall next
  year than to rise again, but this mean reversion is weak.
* **Logistic regression, lasso and LDA are joint best** (CV AUC about 0.68), and almost identical. The lasso's best
  penalty is so small (λ ≈ 0.00003) that it is effectively plain logistic regression: no feature is worth dropping.
* **The flexible models do not help.** The random forest (0.645), QDA (0.649), KNN (0.626) and the tree (0.60) are
  all below the linear models. KNN's best *k* is very large (301 neighbours out of about 1,000 training rows), so it
  wants to average over a third of the data, not over close neighbours. The forest prefers its most restricted
  settings (`mtry` = 2, large leaves). Both point to a weak, mostly linear signal with little local or interaction
  structure for flexible models to exploit.
* The tree's best `cp` is the smallest value tried, which means a large tree. Yet its CV AUC is almost the same at
  every `cp` (about 0.60), so a single tree is unstable here whatever its size.

## Choosing a model

As in RQ1, we take the best CV AUC, subtract one standard error, and choose the **simplest** model above that line.
Models are ordered from simplest to most flexible as in the table above (baselines are not candidates).

```{r one-se}
candidates <- cv_all |> filter(!model %in% c("Majority class", "Same as this year", "Opposite of this year"))
best_row  <- candidates |> slice_max(cv_auc, n = 1)
threshold <- best_row$cv_auc - best_row$cv_auc_se
chosen <- candidates |> filter(cv_auc >= threshold) |> arrange(model) |> slice(1)
candidates |> mutate(within_1se = cv_auc >= threshold) |> select(model, cv_auc, cv_auc_se, within_1se) |>
  kable(digits = 3)
c(best = as.character(best_row$model), threshold = round(threshold, 3), chosen = as.character(chosen$model))
```

**Observation.** Logistic regression, lasso, LDA, QDA and the random forest are all within one standard
error of the best. The fold-to-fold variation is large because each fold validates on only two years, and each
year behaves differently. Following the rule, we choose the simplest: **plain logistic regression**. It has no
tuning, its coefficients are interpretable as odds ratios, and it is one of the two models the pitch named.

# Test-set evaluation (2017–2024)

Each model is refitted at its tuned settings on all training years and scored once on the 528 test district-years.

```{r test-eval, cache = TRUE}
fps <- list("Majority class" = fp_majority, "Same as this year" = fp_same, "Opposite of this year" = fp_opposite,
            "Logistic regression" = fp_logistic, "Lasso logistic" = fp_lasso, "LDA" = fp_lda, "QDA" = fp_qda,
            "Classification tree" = fp_tree, "k-nearest neighbours" = fp_knn, "Random forest" = fp_rf)
test_prob <- imap_dfr(fps, function(fp, m) {
  best <- as.list(res[[m]]$best)
  p <- as.matrix(fp(train, test, best))
  if (m == "Lasso logistic") p <- p[, which.min(abs(as.numeric(colnames(p)) - best$lambda)), drop = FALSE]
  tibble(model = m, row = seq_len(nrow(test)), prob = as.numeric(p))
})
```

```{r test-table}
test_long <- test_prob |>
  left_join(test |> mutate(row = row_number()) |> select(row, ta, year, rise, nat_rise_next), by = "row")
test_res <- test_long |>
  group_by(model) |>
  summarise(class_metrics(rise, prob), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(cv_all |> select(model, cv_auc) |> mutate(model = as.character(model)), by = "model") |>
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels = model_order)) |>
  arrange(model)
tv <- function(m, col = "auc") test_res[[col]][test_res$model == m]
save_tab(test_res, "t04_test_results", dir = paths$tab_rq3) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Test years 2017–2024 (outcomes 2018–2025): every model at its tuned settings")
```

```{r roc, fig.height = 4.6}
roc_models <- c("Logistic regression", "LDA", "Classification tree", "Random forest", "Opposite of this year")
roc_df <- test_long |> filter(model %in% roc_models) |>
  group_by(model) |> group_modify(\(d, k) roc_points(d$rise, d$prob)) |> ungroup() |>
  left_join(test_res |> transmute(model = as.character(model), auc), by = "model") |>
  mutate(label = sprintf("%s (AUC %.2f)", model, auc))
p_roc <- ggplot(roc_df, aes(fpr, tpr, colour = label)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = 2, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_step(linewidth = 0.8) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "ROC curves on the test years",
       subtitle = "Each point is a threshold. The diagonal is random guessing.",
       x = "False positive rate (1 − specificity)", y = "True positive rate (sensitivity)", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
save_fig(p_roc, "fig04_roc_test", dir = paths$fig_rq3, height = 4.6, width = 8)
```

```{r confusion}
conf <- test_long |> filter(model == as.character(chosen$model)) |>
  mutate(predicted = if_else(prob > 0.5, "rise", "fall"), actual = if_else(rise == 1, "rise", "fall"))
table(Predicted = conf$predicted, Actual = conf$actual)
```

**Observation.** * **Logistic regression is right on about 58% of test district-years**, with AUC
`r round(tv("Logistic regression"), 2)`. This is clearly better than every baseline: always predicting "rise"
(48%), "same direction" (47%) or "opposite direction" (53%). But it is a modest improvement over guessing.
* LDA and lasso perform the same as logistic regression. KNN has the same AUC but leans towards predicting "rise"
  (sensitivity 0.75, specificity 0.39). The random forest is no better than the linear models, and the single tree
  is barely better than chance (AUC `r round(tv("Classification tree"), 2)`).
* All test AUCs are lower than in cross-validation (about 0.63 vs 0.68). The test years include the sharpest turn
  in the series, from the 2021 boom to the 2023–24 fall.
* **Confusion matrix (logistic):**
  * it correctly predicts 166 of the 252 actual rises (sensitivity 0.66);
  * it correctly predicts 142 of the 276 actual falls (specificity 0.51);
  * it calls a rise too often, which matches the year-by-year analysis below.
* **Brier score:** logistic regression scores 0.24, compared with 0.25 for always saying 50%. The probabilities carry
  only a little information, so they should be read as "slightly more likely than not", not as confident forecasts.

# Where the model succeeds and fails: year by year

```{r by-year, fig.height = 4}
year_df <- test_long |> filter(model == as.character(chosen$model)) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(actual_share = mean(rise), predicted_share = mean(prob > 0.5), mean_prob = mean(prob),
            accuracy = mean((prob > 0.5) == rise), within_year_auc = auc(rise, prob), .groups = "drop")

p_by_year <- year_df |>
  pivot_longer(c(actual_share, mean_prob), names_to = "series") |>
  mutate(series = recode(series, actual_share = "Actual share rising", mean_prob = "Mean predicted probability")) |>
  ggplot(aes(year + 1, value, colour = series)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Actual share rising" = "black", "Mean predicted probability" = "#e76f51")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2018:2025) +
  labs(title = paste0(chosen$model, ": predicted vs actual share of districts rising"),
       x = "Outcome year", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
save_fig(p_by_year, "fig05_test_by_year", dir = paths$fig_rq3, height = 4)
year_df |> mutate(year = year + 1) |> rename(outcome_year = year) |> kable(digits = 3)
c(mean_within_year_auc = mean(year_df$within_year_auc))
```

**Observation.** This figure shows why RQ3 is hard.

* **The model follows the national direction only weakly.** It predicted more rises than falls in 2021 (correct),
  but its average probability (63%) was far below the 88% that actually rose. In 2023 and 2024 it leaned towards
  falls (47% and 41%) when only 18–23% of districts rose.
* **It misses turning points.** For 2018 it predicted rises for 92% of districts, when only half rose. For 2025 it
  predicted mostly falls (27% predicted to rise), and 62% rose. The national features describe where the cycle
  *is*, but not reliably when it will *turn*.
* **Within a year, ranking is weak but real.** In each year separately, the AUC averages
  `r round(mean(year_df$within_year_auc), 2)`. Given the national direction, the model can only slightly pick out
  which districts are more likely to rise.
* Accuracy by year ranges from 47% to 76%. It is best in years when most districts move the same way as the model
  expects, and worst at turning points.

# What drives the predictions?

## Logistic regression: odds ratios

Logistic regression models the **log-odds** of a rise:

$$
\log\frac{P(\text{rise})}{1 - P(\text{rise})} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_{11} x_{11}.
$$

The **odds** are P(rise) ÷ P(fall): odds of 1 mean 50:50, odds of 2 mean a rise is twice as likely as a fall. With
standardised features, e^β is the **odds ratio** for a one-standard-deviation increase in that feature, holding
the others fixed. An odds ratio above 1 makes a rise more likely, below 1 less likely.

```{r odds-ratios, fig.height = 4}
train_std <- train |> mutate(across(all_of(feats), \(x) as.numeric(scale(x))))
logit_std <- glm(fml, data = train_std, family = binomial)
or_tab <- summary(logit_std)$coefficients[-1, ] |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "feature") |>
  transmute(feature, estimate = Estimate, se = `Std. Error`, p_value = `Pr(>|z|)`,
            odds_ratio = exp(estimate), lower = exp(estimate - 1.96 * se), upper = exp(estimate + 1.96 * se)) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(estimate)))
save_tab(or_tab, "t05_odds_ratios", dir = paths$tab_rq3) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Logistic regression (training years): odds ratio for a 1-SD increase, with 95% interval")

p_or <- ggplot(or_tab, aes(odds_ratio, fct_reorder(feature, odds_ratio))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = odds_ratio > 1), size = 2.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#e76f51", `FALSE` = "#2a6f97")) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "Logistic regression: odds of a rise next year, per 1-SD increase",
       subtitle = "Bars = 95% confidence intervals (optimistic: district-years are not independent)",
       x = "Odds ratio (log scale)", y = NULL)
save_fig(p_or, "fig06_odds_ratios", dir = paths$fig_rq3, height = 4)
```

**Observation.** The three **national** features have the largest effects:

* **`nat_dev_5y`** (odds ratio about 1.8 per SD): when New Zealand is building above its five-year average, districts
  are more likely to rise again. The national cycle has momentum over one year.
* **`nat_h2_vs_h1`** (about 1.7): a strong second half of the year nationally points to a rise next year.
* **`nat_growth_1y`** (about 0.6): *holding the other two fixed*, a big national jump this year makes a rise next
  year less likely. Together with the first two, the model reads "high and still building momentum" as rising, and
  "a sudden jump" as likely to cool.

District features have smaller effects:

* a higher **multi-unit share** lowers the odds (0.75), because apartment and townhouse projects come in lumps;
* stronger **alteration growth** (1.27) and a stronger **second half** in the district (1.26) raise them;
* higher **building intensity** (0.82) and being **above the district's own five-year average** (0.82) lower them
  (mean reversion);
* non-residential growth has no detectable effect.

The confidence intervals assume independent rows. District-years in the same year are strongly linked through the
national cycle, so the intervals are too narrow. We read the odds ratios as directions and rough sizes, not as
precise tests.

## LDA: the discriminant direction

LDA finds the single combination of features along which the two classes are furthest apart, relative to their
spread. Its coefficients (`scaling`) give that direction. On standardised features they are comparable in size.

```{r lda}
lda_std <- lda(fml, data = train_std)
tibble(feature = rownames(lda_std$scaling), LD1 = lda_std$scaling[, 1]) |>
  left_join(or_tab |> select(feature, logistic_coef = estimate), by = "feature") |>
  arrange(desc(abs(LD1))) |> kable(digits = 3, caption = "LDA coefficients vs logistic coefficients (standardised features)")
lda_std$prior
```

**Observation.** The LDA coefficients are almost exactly proportional to the logistic coefficients (each about
1.3 times larger) and rank the features in the same order. This is expected. With two classes, both methods produce
a straight-line boundary in the features, and they differ only in how they estimate it:

* **logistic regression** maximises the likelihood of the observed rises and falls directly;
* **LDA** assumes each class is a normal cloud with the same covariance matrix and applies Bayes' rule.

When the assumptions roughly hold, or the signal is weak, they agree, which is why their test results are almost
identical. QDA drops the equal-covariance assumption and fits a curved boundary, but with a weak signal the extra
flexibility mostly adds noise (lower AUC, worse Brier score). The priors (47% fall, 53% rise) are the class shares
in the training data.

## Classification tree

```{r tree-plot, fig.height = 5, out.width = "100%"}
bt <- res[["Classification tree"]]$best
tree_fit <- rpart(update(fml, factor(rise) ~ .), data = train, method = "class",
                  control = rpart.control(cp = 0.02, minbucket = bt$minbucket, xval = 0))   # pruned harder so it can be read
draw_tree <- function() rpart.plot(tree_fit, type = 2, extra = 104, under = TRUE, roundint = FALSE,
                                   box.palette = "BuRd", main = "Classification tree (pruned for display): fall vs rise next year")
png(file.path(paths$fig_rq3, "fig07_tree.png"), width = 10, height = 5.5, units = "in", res = 200)
draw_tree(); invisible(dev.off())
draw_tree()
```

**Observation.** The tree's first split is on **national end-of-year momentum** (`nat_h2_vs_h1`).
* **When the national second half was more than about 22% busier than the first** (24% of rows), 71% of districts rose
  the next year.
* **Otherwise**, it splits on whether the national level is well below its five-year average. In those years (10% of
  rows), only 16% of districts rose.
* Further down, it uses building intensity, the multi-unit share and the district's own momentum.

The splits tell the same story as the logistic regression. But a single tree turns these weak signals into hard
thresholds that change a lot from sample to sample, which is why its test AUC is close to 0.5.

# A check: removing the national cycle

Most of the difficulty comes from the national cycle. Following RQ1's relative-cost idea, we also try a **relative**
label: did the district's new dwellings grow **faster than the rest of New Zealand's** next year? This removes the
national direction from the label, so only district differences are left to predict. We fit logistic regression on
the district features only (the national ones are the same for every district in a year and cannot help).

```{r relative}
add_relative <- function(df) {
  df |> group_by(year) |>
    mutate(tot = sum(dwellings), next_tot = sum(next_dwellings)) |> ungroup() |>
    mutate(g_district = log((next_dwellings + 1) / (dwellings + 1)),
           g_rest     = log((next_tot - next_dwellings) / (tot - dwellings)),
           outperform = as.integer(g_district > g_rest))
}
dat_rel <- add_relative(dat)
district_feats <- setdiff(feats, c("nat_growth_1y", "nat_dev_5y", "nat_h2_vs_h1"))
fml_rel <- reformulate(district_feats, "outperform")
rel_fit <- glm(fml_rel, data = dat_rel |> filter(split == "train"), family = binomial)
rel_test <- dat_rel |> filter(split == "test")
rel_prob <- predict(rel_fit, rel_test, type = "response")
bind_rows(class_metrics(rel_test$outperform, rel_prob) |> mutate(model = "Logistic, relative label"),
          class_metrics(rel_test$outperform, rep(mean(dat_rel$outperform[dat_rel$split == "train"]), nrow(rel_test))) |>
            mutate(model = "Majority class, relative label")) |>
  select(model, accuracy, balanced_accuracy, auc, brier) |> kable(digits = 3)
```

**Observation.** Removing the national cycle does **not** make the problem easier. With the relative label
("did the district beat the rest of NZ?"), logistic regression on the district features reaches AUC
`r round(auc(rel_test$outperform, rel_prob), 2)`, lower than for the original label. District features carry only a
small amount of information about next year, whichever way the label is defined. The national features add the
most, but they can't fully predict the national turning points.

# Answer to RQ3

**Question.** Will a district's consents rise or fall next year?

**Answer.** Only slightly better than a coin toss, using the consents data alone.

* The best model, **logistic regression**, predicts the direction correctly for about **58%** of district-years in
  2018–2025 (AUC 0.63). This beats every simple rule (48–53%). LDA and lasso logistic regression do equally well.
  More flexible models (random forest, KNN, QDA, a single tree) do not do better.
* The main reason is that **districts rise and fall together** with the national building cycle. The share of
  districts rising ranges from 12% to 88% depending on the year. Our features describe where the national cycle is,
  but they can't reliably predict when it turns (2018, 2025).
* **What raises the odds of a rise:**
  * the country building above its five-year average, with a strong second half of the year;
  * locally, growing renovation spending and a strong end to the year.
* **What lowers them:** a sudden national jump, a high share of apartments and townhouses (lumpy projects), high
  building intensity, and a district above its own recent average (mean reversion).
* Even within a year, the model ranks districts only slightly better than chance (AUC about 0.59).

**Limitations.**

* The consents data contain no economic drivers: interest rates, migration, house prices and credit conditions are
  what turn the national cycle. Adding them would be the most promising next step.
* District-years in the same year are not independent, so the odds-ratio intervals are optimistic.
* Small districts have noisy year-to-year counts, which no model can predict.

| Model | Test accuracy | Test AUC | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Always "rise" (majority class) | 48% | 0.50 | baseline |
| Opposite of this year | 53% | 0.53 | best simple rule |
| **Logistic regression** | **58%** | **0.63** | chosen (simplest within 1 SE) |
| LDA | 58% | 0.63 | same boundary as logistic |
| Random forest | 58% | 0.62 | no gain from flexibility |
| Classification tree | 53% | 0.52 | unstable |

# Save

```{r save}
final_fit <- glm(fml, data = dat, family = binomial)    # chosen model refitted on all years, for later use
saveRDS(list(cv = cv_all, test = test_res, chosen = chosen, test_predictions = test_long,
             odds_ratios = or_tab, by_year = year_df,
             final_logistic = final_fit, features = feats,
             latest = dat |> filter(year == max(year))),
        file.path(paths$models_rq3, "rq3_results.rds"))
list.files(paths$models_rq3)
```
